title: Cap. 4 Mem. 1 Rat. 4 and close: Piscator/Pareus; intent vs ordination; first member closed
pass_a_gloss: Rat.4: From confession of restrictivists themselves, bare in-se sufficiency can’t make true ‘Christ died sufficienter for all.’ Piscator Resp.Apolog.87: cannot say sufficienter for all — would follow died for all, contrary demonstrated; distinction sufficienter/efficaciter empty (contradiction). Indeed contradiction if admit bare sufficiency for all yet deny universal ordination to procure all’s salvation — must explode orthodox distinction OR with us acknowledge ordinata sufficiency to free all. Pareus: Christ re meriti sufficientia died & willed to die for all & each — not only intrinsic value but will of dying Christ ordaining death sufficiently to free all. Note error of those who restrict death to elect-only will yet claim no question about sufficiency for all & each, controversy only about efficacious act. Even with in-se sufficiency for 1000 worlds + efficacy destined absolutely only to certain persons, still controversial whether death has only hypothetical intrinsic sufficiency OR also conjunct Divine ordination by which this in-se-sufficient lytron was de facto offered for all & thence applicable/to-be-applied to all if they submit to that ordination. We defend such ordination even toward those not saved because they believed not in the only-begotten’s name → hence sufficienter dead for all. Some elect-only advocates seem to defend not bare but ordinata from God’s intention. Ames-type: ‘PRO OMNIBUS’ admitted for sufficiency & God’s intention that it be sufficient for all — improper locution but with fundamentum in re. Others: Father’s counsel that Christ pay such lytron as in itself would suffice to reconcile all. Seem to add intention-related sufficiency — but don’t really. (1) Intention that death be sufficient is of no moment — infinite value needs no added intention to be sufficient; needs intention/ordination to be given & accepted for freeing all under any condition. Sufficientia=intrinsic potentia/aptitudo; ordination to free persons=voluntary act from ordinantis counsel. Frivolous to couple God’s intention with internal rei sufficiency — intention either denied for sufficienter-for-all OR joined to ordination toward all. (2) Claim phrase has fundamentum in re fails on their view: ‘death is sufficient lytron for all’ rests on dying Person’s dignity; but ‘Christ is sufficienter dead/offered on cross for all’ (equipollent) has no truth-ground unless first he suffered/offered for all, then add lytron-dignity sufficiency. Who denies the one vainly defends the other. Conclusion: neither truly said sufficienter dead for all, nor death truly universal applicable remedy per God’s ordination, unless besides mere sufficiency from innate dignity we admit from God’s accepting will & Christ’s offering a stable decree by which this death can bring eternal life to all & each. Hactenus first member: bare sufficiency in death per se does not suffice for ‘died for all’ or universal cause of salvation for whole race. Next: what further is required — second thesis serves.
pass_b_english: 4. We prove that a bare sufficiency of the thing offered in itself cannot make true that pronouncement of the Theologians, Christ died sufficiently for all human beings, and that from the confession of those who deny that Christ’s death was spent on the whole human race and restrict it to the elect alone. So Piscator in the Apologetic Response, section 87: It cannot be said that Christ died sufficiently for all: for it would follow that he died for all, whose contrary has been demonstrated. And in the same place, that distinction by which Christ is said to have died for all sufficiently, for the elect alone efficaciously, is empty, because it implies a contradiction, etc. It truly implies a contradiction among those who admit a bare sufficiency of the death as to all, and utterly deny its universal ordination for procuring the salvation of all human beings. They are therefore bound either to explode this distinction hitherto approved by the orthodox, or with us to acknowledge an ordained sufficiency of Christ’s death for freeing all. The most learned Pareus seems to go this way when he affirms that Christ, as to the sufficiency of his merit, died and willed to die for all and each. Where he does not constitute this sufficiency in that alone, that Christ’s death in its intrinsic value suffices for redeeming all; but also in the will of Christ dying and sufficiently ordaining his death to freeing all. And here it is to be noted in passing that those err who narrow Christ’s death to the elect alone, so as to establish that he willed to die for them alone, and yet plead that there is no question or contention about the sufficiency of Christ’s death for all and each; that the whole controversy is about the act of this efficacy. For even with that sufficiency of the death in itself for redeeming a thousand worlds posited; and this also posited, that the efficacy of this death is destined absolutely and infallibly not to all but to certain persons to be freed in fact — still it remains controversial whether Christ’s death has only an intrinsic sufficiency for redeeming all, conceived under the hypothesis, If he had willed to offer and pay that lytron for all, or also a conjunct Divine ordination according to which this lytron, sufficient in itself, was in fact offered for all, and thence is applicable and to be applied to all unto salvation, if they have been willing to obey and subject themselves to the aforesaid ordination. Such an ordination we defend, looking even to those who are not saved, because they did not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God; and hence we say that Christ died sufficiently for all. But here some of those who hold tightly that Christ suffered and died for the elect alone nevertheless wish to seem to defend not a bare sufficiency of Christ’s death in itself, but that ordained one from God’s intention which we assert. And for this reason, when they are pressed with arguments, they do not refuse to mention the Divine will and intention. Their mind and sense must be examined more closely, lest we seem to wrestle with ghosts, or to fight (as they say) about goat’s wool.

So a certain learned man wrote on this matter: When we confess that Christ died for all, that phrase, FOR ALL, is admitted by our men on account of the sufficiency and the intention of God, by which he willed that it be sufficient for all. Yet it is to be known that this locution is improper; not however to be rejected, because it sometimes has a foundation in the thing itself, and among Theologians is received by long use. Others say in the same sense that it was the counsel and decree of God the Father that by his passion and death Christ should pay such a lytron as, considered in itself, would suffice for reconciling all human beings. These seem, besides a mere sufficiency of the thing, to add a sufficiency related and pertaining from God’s intention and counsel to reconciling all human beings. They seem to, but in truth they do not. For first, that they say they acknowledge Christ to have died sufficiently for all on account of God’s intention by which he willed that his death be sufficient for all, is of no moment. For the death of the Son of God does not need some supervening intention in order to be sufficient for all, since in itself it is of infinite value: yet it does need, in order to be given and accepted for freeing them, under whatever condition. Sufficiency is a certain intrinsic power and aptitude of the thing: nor is an extrinsic act of one intending this sufficiency required to constitute it; but ordination to freeing any persons is a voluntary act, and flows from the intention and counsel of the one ordaining. It is therefore frivolous to couple God’s intention with the internal sufficiency of the thing; which intention was either to be denied altogether as to Christ having died sufficiently for all, or was to be joined with an ordination of the death pertaining to all. Second, that they say this phrase, Christ died sufficiently for all, has a foundation in the thing, cannot be defended on their own view. If I should say, Christ’s death is a sufficient lytron for all, the true foundation of this saying is in the thing itself, namely in the dignity of the dying Person: but if I say, Christ is sufficiently dead or offered on the altar of the cross for all (which are equipollent), there is now no foundation on which the truth of this saying stands, unless I first posit that Christ suffered and was offered for all, and then also add the sufficiency of this passion for all from the dignity of the lytron. He who denies the one forum vainly attempts to defend the saying in the other. Let us conclude, then, that neither can Christ truly be said to have suffered or died sufficiently for all, nor can Christ’s death truly be acknowledged as a universal remedy applicable to all human beings according to God’s ordination, unless besides a mere sufficiency of the thing flowing from its innate dignity we admit, from the will of God accepting this victim and of Christ offering the same, a stable and fixed decree of God according to which this death of Christ can bring eternal life to all and each. And thus far we have treated the first member of our thesis: in which we have shown that that bare sufficiency which is understood in Christ’s death itself considered by itself does not suffice for this, that Christ be said to have died for all, or that his death be held the universal cause of salvation with respect to the whole human race. Let us show further what that is which is required beyond this for the matter. This second thesis will serve to illustrate that point.
source_text: 4. Probamus nudam rei oblatae in se sufficientiam non posse verum reddere illud pronunciatum Theologorum, Christus pro omnibus hominibus mortuus est sufficienter, idque ex confessione eorum qui mortem Christi toti humano generi impensam negant, et ad solos electos restringunt. Sic Piscator in Resp. Apologet. Sect. 87, Dici non potest, Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter: sequeretur enim mortuum esse pro omnibus, cujus contrarium est demonstratum. Et eodem in loco, distinctio illa qua dicitur Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse sufficienter, pro solis electis efficaciter, inanis est, quia implicat contradictionem, etc. Revera implicat contradictionem apud illos qui nudam mortis sufficientiam quoad omnes admittunt, et ordinationem ejus universalem ad omnium hominum salutem procurandam pernegant. Tenentur igitur hanc distinctionem hactenus ab orthodoxis probatam explodere, aut nobiscum ordinatam mortis Christi ad omnes liberandos sufficientiam agnoscere. Doctissimus Pareus in hanc sententiam ire videtur, quando affirmat, Christum quoad sufficientiam meriti sui, pro omnibus et singulis mortuum esse, et mori voluisse. Ubi hanc sufficientiam non in eo solo constituit, quod mors Christi in suo valore intrinseco sufficiat ad omnes redimendos; sed in voluntate etiam Christi morientis, ac mortem suam ad omnes liberandos sufficienter ordinantis. Atqui hic obiter notandum est, falli eos qui arctant mortem Christi ad solos electos, ita ut pro illis solis mori voluisse statuant, et tamen obtendant, De sufficientia mortis Christi pro omnibus et singulis nullam esse quaestionem aut contentionem; controversiam vero omnem esse de actu hujus efficaciae. Nam posita illa sufficientia mortis in se ad mille mundos redimendos; et hoc etiam posito, quod mortis hujus efficacia non ad omnes sed ad certas quasdam personas de facto liberandas absolute et infallibiliter destinetur, tamen adhuc manet controversum, Utrum mors Christi intrinsecam sufficientiam ad omnes redimendos, sub hypothesi nempe conceptam, Si pro omnibus illud lytron offerre et solvere voluisset, non habeat, etiam conjunctam Dei ordinationem, juxta quam hoc lytron in se sufficiens, pro omnibus de facto oblatum fuit, atque inde omnibus ad salutem applicabile atque applicandum, si praedictae ordinationi parere ac sese subjicere voluerint. Talem ordinationem nos tuemur, etiam ad illos spectantem qui non servantur, quia non crediderunt in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei; atque hinc dicimus Christum pro omnibus sufficienter mortuum. Sed hic nonnulli ex illis qui Christum pro solis electis passum et mortuum acriter tenent, nihilo tamen minus videri volunt non nudam mortis Christi in se sufficientiam, sed illam ordinatam ex Dei intentione quam nos asserimus, defendere. Atque hanc ob causam, cum urgentur argumentis, voluntatis et intentionis Divinae mentionem facere non recusant. Quorum mens et sententia propius excutienda est, ne cum larvis luctari, aut de lana (quod aiunt) caprina pugnare videamur. Sic igitur doctus quidam vir hac de re scripsit, Quando fatemur Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse, phrasis illa, PRO OMNIBUS, a nostris propter sufficientiam et intentionem Dei, qua voluit ut sit sufficiens pro omnibus, admittitur. Sciendum tamen est impropriam hanc locutionem esse; non rejiciendam tamen, quia fundamentum aliquando in re ipsa habet, et apud Theologos est usu longe recepta. Alii in eandem sententiam aiunt, Consilium et decretum Dei Patris fuisse ut Christus passione et morte sua ejusmodi lytron persolveret, quod in se consideratum omnibus hominibus reconciliandis sufficeret. Videntur hi, praeter meram rei sufficientiam, addere sufficientiam ex intentione et consilio Dei ad omnes homines reconciliandos relatam et pertinentem. Videntur quidem sed revera non faciunt. Nam primo quod aiunt se agnoscere Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter propter intentionem Dei, qua voluit ut mors ejus sit sufficiens pro omnibus, nullius momenti est. Mors siquidem Filii Dei non eget superveniente aliqua intentione ut sit sufficiens pro omnibus, cum in se sit valoris infiniti: eget tamen, ut sit pro omnibus data et acceptata ad eos liberandos, sub quacunque conditione. Sufficientia est intrinseca quaedam potentia et aptitudo rei: nec requiritur ad illam constituendam extrinsecus actus intendentis hanc sufficientiam; sed ordinatio ad personas quascunque liberandas, est actus voluntarius, et fluit ab intentione et consilio ordinantis. Frivolum itaque copulare intentionem Dei cum interna sufficientia rei; quae intentio aut omnino neganda fuit quoad Christum pro omnibus sufficienter mortuum; aut cum ordinatione mortis ad omnes pertinente fuit conjungenda. Secundo quod dicunt hanc phrasin, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter, habere fundamentum in re, ex ipsorum sententia defendi non potest. Si dicerem, Christi mors est sufficiens lytron pro omnibus, est hujus dicti verum fundamentum in ipsa re, nempe in dignitate personae morientis: at si dicam, Christus est pro omnibus sufficienter mortuus vel oblatus in ara crucis (quae sunt aequipollentia), jam nullum est fundamentum in quo subsistit hujus dicti veritas, nisi primo ponam Christum pro omnibus passum et oblatum, dein et adjungam hujus passionis pro omnibus ex dignitate lytri sufficientiam. Forum unum qui negat, frustra in altero ejus dicti defensionem tentat. Concludamus ergo, quod neque Christus vere dici potest pro omnibus passus sive mortuus sufficienter, neque mors Christi vere agnosci universale remedium omnibus hominibus juxta ordinationem Dei applicabile, nisi praeter meram sufficientiam rei ex innata ejus dignitate fluentem, admittamus ex voluntate Dei hanc hostiam acceptantis et Christi eandem offerentis, stabile et fixum Dei decretum juxta quod omnibus et singulis haec mors Christi vitam aeternam possit apportare. Atque hactenus primum membrum thesis nostrae tractavimus: In quo ostendimus, nudam illam sufficientiam, quae in ipsa morte Christi per se considerata intelligitur, non ad hoc sufficere ut Christus pro omnibus mortuus dicatur, aut ut mors ejus universalis causa salutis respectu totius humani generis habeatur. Ostendamus porro quid illud sit quod ad hanc rem ultra requiratur. Huic rei illustrandae secunda haec thesis inserviet.
